title: Water with Chris Kaputo
body:
Life’s uncertainties bring us through distinct phases, some of which we invite, others we wish to deter. Water takes on new forms dependent upon its conditions, becoming what it needs to evolve. Just as the essence of water remains when it takes on a different state, so do the centres of who we are through personal change. The work delved into will open up the space to consider the functions of water, through its properties of cleansing and renewal. Its fluidity reminds us there are unmarked pathways that can be created and taken in the face of stagnancy. The expansiveness of water helps us to look beyond what is readily apparent, and invites us to be attentive to our own depths, and our ability to transform. 

Our final session will be facilitated by featured poet, Christopher Kaputo and Tender Possibilities’ founder, Farhia Tato.

Christopher Kaputo (he/him) is a Congolese poet/multidisciplinary artist based in Tkaronto. Through the art of written and spoken word, he introduces an honest perspective of his upbringing, rooted in a humanity that he hopes can become a shared experience that brings people together despite differences. He uses poetry as a means to connect, remember and transform the ways we relate to ourselves and others.
This series is made possible with support from City of Toronto and Scarborough Arts. With special thanks to our community partners: Toronto Public Library and East Scarborough Storefront
Flyer and program designed by Anda Untila
Refreshments will be served by Krish Dineshkumar

title: Fire with Maneesa Veeravel
body: Fire has the ability to create or wreck, transforming that which it comes into contact with. Ecological collapse has accelerated the scope of its devastation, its brunt most heavily faced by marginalized communities. While the intensity of fire demands reckoning, its heat can also reshape, or forge something anew. As the structures of the everyday become more precarious, fire casts its light over what must be faced to move forward. When a way of life collapses in on itself, how do we imagine ourselves in the aftermath? Just as it can make or destroy, fire also nurtures, the hearth standing as an emblem; a beacon of communal gathering signalling to what lies beyond the immediacy of upheaval. The poems explored will bring together the multiple poles of fire's capabilities and what can be gleaned from its variances.
This session will be facilitated by featured poet, Maneesa Veeraval and Tender Possibilities’ founder, Farhia Tato.

Maneesa Veeravel is an interdisciplinary artist whose practice moves across poetry, visual art, and community-based creation. A mad, queer, Tamil, gender fluid, survivor, Maneesa was born and settled on the stolen lands of the Wendat, Anishinaabe, Mississaugas of the Credit, and Haudenosaunee peoples. Through art, research, and collective learning, their work gathers intergenerational wits, wounds, and wisdoms, tending to questions of land, body, memory, and the ongoing practice of survival.
Presented with support from the City of Toronto and Scarborough Arts, with special thanks to our community partner East Scarborough Storefront
Flyer and program designed by Anda Untila

title: Regards Noirs Festival with Chorus in Motion
image_alt: Regards Noirs Festival with Chorus in Motion
body: Workshop #1: A participatory poetry exploration with A Chorus in Motion (Belen Blizzard) + Tender Possibilities (Farhia Tato) 🎭✨

We will explore the jester as the complex character behind the mask, moving through the intersections of humor and tragedy, hidden wisdom, social critique and vulnerability. The jester is the often-entertaining force meant to distract the populace from the dread. The jester subverts truth and emboldens those needing and wishing for destruction. This force or being feels very powerful right now, as it also points towards the experience of disillusionment.

Disillusionment is a continuous process of undoing what we hold to be true. It manifests in our political horizons, our relational bonds, and our understanding of our place in the world. The jester ushers us into the space of unlearning; this figure breaks apart antiquated truths, and leaps into the troubling space of the unknown.
We will engage curated poems based on these themes as an attempt to articulate and identify this being and this force.
Free ~ bilingual (French + English) ~ Limited spots.
RSVP here!

title: Earth with Jesse June-Jack
body: What does it mean to gather on earth at a time when so much is ending and how does anything truly end? This session considers earth as a living record of transformation: sediment, moss, bone and the accumulated traces of many eras. Earth insists upon periods of gestation and decomposition, processes that unfold alongside one another rather than in opposition. Working with the ancient technologies of poetry and ritual, we will ask how we might honour what is disappearing while remaining attentive to what is germinating, returning or taking another form.

We’ll collectively explore poems that move across earthly and celestial scales, connecting bodies, landscapes, memory and the stars. We will read work interested in ecological entanglement and poems that blur the boundaries between self and environment, the visible and unseen, life and decay. We will reflect on how language can help us sense the dense web of relations between beings, histories and the places we call home.
This session will be facilitated by featured poet, Jesse June-Jack and Tender Possibilities’ founder, Farhia Tato.

Jesse June-Jack is a Nigerian-Canadian spoken word poet and writer. His poetry can be found in publications such as Poems In Passage on the TTC and anthologies such as A Thousand Tiny Awakenings (published by Lat23 Publishing). He is a part of organizing programs with communities such as Toronto Youth Poetry Slam and collectives such as the Common College of Art. He is also a part of the audiovisual series Dreams In Vantablack on YouTube with CBC Gem, and most recently he released his debut poetry anthology The Universe Is A Beating Heart. Despite all this, he's still figuring out this poetry thing though.
Presented with support from the City of Toronto and our community partners Scarborough Arts and Toronto Public Library - Morningside Branch.
Flyer and program designed by Anda Untila
Refreshments will be served by Zo’s Cuisine

title: Cultural Hotspot Project: Poetry as Gathering in KGO
image_alt: Cultural Hotspot Project: Poetry as Gathering in KGO
body: Join us for Tender Possibilities: Poetry as Gathering in KGO, a three-part series presented in collaboration with Scarborough Arts from August 9 to September 20, 2026.

Moving through elemental themes, each gathering will consider how poetry can deepen our relationship to place, memory and community. Grounding ourselves within nature physically and thematically, presents an opportunity for us to expand our perception of our day to day surroundings. Sessions will take place at different locations throughout the Kingston-Galloway-Orton Park neighbourhood, inviting us to read and reflect alongside the land, histories and lived experiences of KGO. Greater consideration of how our connection to the environment shapes our personal and collective narratives, enlivens our bonds to the places we call home.
Tender Possibilities will host and facilitate the gatherings alongside Scarborough-based featured poets Jesse June-Jack, Maneesa Veeravel and Christopher Kaputo.

All sessions take place from 2–4 PM, with refreshments beginning at 1:30 PM. Individual event registration will open closer to each gathering. Stay connected by subscribing to our newsletter and/or instagram 🤍
This series is made possible with support from City of Toronto and Scarborough Arts. Special thanks to our community partners: Toronto Public Library and East Scarborough Storefront

title: Repair with Danielle Boissoneau
body:
Join us on Saturday January 24th, 2026 from 1:00 to 3:00 PM at Black Oak for a collaborative gathering with Garden of Repairs.

Drawing on anti-colonial traditions of kinship, we'll read and discuss poems that move across imposed borders. These works offer intimate cartographies that counter settler histories and patriarchal geographies. Through ecopoetics, we come to understand that it is not the world’s desires that drive the Earth, but the Earth itself (generous and instructive) guiding us toward deeper attunement. Together, we consider how repair emerges through renewed relationality with one another and the living systems that hold us.

The session is facilitated by Featured Poet Danielle Boissoneau @onedeelikeme and Tender Possibilities’ founder, Farhia Tato.

Danielle Boissoneau enjoys creating new worlds with her words, with hope and with her community. She is a multidisciplinary artist who writes plays and poetry and is continually fascinated by the role of sound and movement throughout our creative practices. Danielle is Anishinaabekwe from Garden River and belongs to the Old Turtle Clan. She currently calls Hamilton home.

title: Practice with Kai Cheng Thom at the 519
image_alt: Practice with Kai Cheng Thom at the 519
body: “We understand the world better if we tremble with it.” - Édouard Glissant
For the final gathering, in collaboration with The 519’s Each Other's Magnitude, we will explore the theme of practice.

Our current political moment is not only dire, it is incoherent. It’s unclear how to organize effectively against the forces we face. We live in a time of deep uncertainty. And still, practice offers a path. It is an ongoing process that calls for reflection, care, and accountability.

Love, abolition, and joy aren’t just concepts — they are practices we return to every day. They are rooted in relationship, in care, in interdependence. Practice allows us to meet ourselves and each other in the where and how of who we are, where we’ve been, and what we are shaping. These are the ways we resist disposability, the ways we show up for one another. It is about being in relationship with spirit, with revolutionary love, and with each other.

In this closing session, we’ll explore poems that invite reflection on the practices that sustain and strengthen our interconnection. This is a space to honour what we’ve built, to celebrate five months in community at The 519, and to imagine how the threads we’ve woven might continue beyond this series.

A nourishing lunch will be served by Krish @cookeduntiltender, and our participatory poetry exploration will be facilitated by Featured Poet Kai Cheng Thom and Tender Possibilities’ founder Farhia Tato.

RSVP here

Kai Cheng Thom is an award-winning writer, performer, and creative arts facilitator based in tkaronto/Toronto whose work delves deeply into the themes of revolutionary love, transformative justice, and healing from collective trauma. Kai Cheng’s work has received multiple literary awards, including the Stonewall Honor Book Award, the Publishing Triangle Award, and the Dayne Ogilvie Prize for LGBT Writers.

**The session is only open to Black, Indigenous and racialized queer people, and priority is given to Two-Spirit, Non-Binary and Trans community members.**

title: Desire with Khashayar Mohammadi at the 519
image_alt: Desire with Khashayar Mohammadi at the 519
body:
Desire resists definition and coherence. It spills over boundaries, entangles itself in language, agency, and power. Desire is a way of orienting ourselves toward something that structures our sense of the possible. But what happens when that attachment becomes unstable? When the thing we long for cannot or will not materialize?

At times, desire feels like an impulse to reclaim our dignity and the right to shape our own lives. When does desire open pathways, and when does it trap us in loops of expectation and disappointment? How do we navigate the contradictions?

Poetry has long been a space for exploring these tensions. Desire reveals our dependencies, liberates us and marks the limits of what we can hold onto. Through collective readings and discussions, we will reflect on how poets shape desire—how it fuels us, betrays us, and binds us to the world.


This Sunday’s session will be facilitated by featured poet Khashayar Mohammadi @dearkestrel and Tender Possibilities’ founder, Farhia Tato.

Khashayar “Kess” Mohammadi (They/Them) is a queer, Iranian-born, Toronto-based poet, writer, and translator. They are the winner of the 2021 Vallum Poetry Prize. Their fifth poetry manuscript "Book of Interruptions" is forthcoming from Wolsak and Wynn Fall 2025.

**The session is only open to Black, Indigenous and racialized queer people, and priority is given to Two-Spirit, Non-Binary and Trans community members.**

title: Questions with Courtnay McFarlane at the 519
image_alt: Questions with Courtnay McFarlane at the 519
body:
For the upcoming session, we will explore the theme of questions—how they challenge norms, provoke curiosity, and open spaces for reflection; questions we didn’t know we wanted or needed to ask. At all levels of the human experience, there is an absence of essential, meaningful questioning, and it seems that asking tough questions has fallen out of favour. Yet, the questions we ask—and the way in which we ask them—reveal a lot about who we are. This session will focus on how poetry can serve as a tool for meaningful processing, and reflecting on how questions act as mirrors, metaphors, challenge certainty, and open up new possibilities for relation and change. Through this, we will explore how curiosity and inquiry deepen our understanding of ourselves, our histories, and the world, enriching insights and fostering collective reflection.

Before our reading and reflection, we’ll be screening ¿Qué es para usted la poesía? / What Is Poetry to You?—a short film by Cecilia Vicuña. This session will be facilitated by featured poet Courtnay McFarlane @guineps and Tender Possibilities’ founder, Farhia Tato.

Courtnay McFarlane is a Jamaican-born and Toronto-based visual artist, curator and poet whose literary work has been published in African-Canadian and Queer anthologies. A long-time activist in Toronto’s Black LGBTQ communities, he was a founding member of a number of groups that were forerunners in providing voice and visibility to Black LGBTQ issues.

**The session is only open to Black, Indigenous and racialized queer people, and priority is given to Two-Spirit, Non-Binary and Trans community members.**

title: Afterlife with Leon Tsai at the 519
image_alt: Afterlife with Leon Tsai at the 519
body: "According to other beings above this sphere of existence, they don't regard this here as life; they consider this planet as the planet of death, & they don't bother with life or death." – Sun Ra

What lies beyond the veil? This session invites participants to explore the afterlife not as an endpoint, but as a continuum — a shift into something vast, interconnected, and unseen. Inspired by Sun Ra’s cosmic perspective, we will examine death as part of a greater transformation, a dimension where life and death intertwine and become something beyond both.

Through a curated selection of poetry, we will reflect on what it means to live, to die, and to be part of the enduring mystery. The poems will serve as bridges between what we perceive as existence and the unknown, exploring themes of impermanence, connection, and the eternal cycle. We invite participants to consider life and death as a threshold — a fragile pause between infinite unknowables.
This session will be facilitated by featured poet Leon Tsai and Tender Possibilities’ founder, Farhia Tato.

Leon (they/she) is a Taiwanese trans-femme and settler-immigrant storyteller (un/re)learning in Tkaronto. While seeding softness through grief and madness, they invite the world on this journey together: planning, caring, and preparing for the softest revolution yet where none is left behind. May we blossom softer, so we don’t break further.

title: Witness with Jedidiah Mugarura at The 519
image_alt: Witness with Jedidiah Mugarura at The 519
body: We’re excited to announce a collaboration between The 519’s Each Other’s Magnitude Project: 2SQTBIPOC Intergenerational Storytelling and Tender Possibilities, a participatory poetry and creative placemaking initiative. This partnership will focus on highlighting the voices and experiences of intergenerational QTBIPOC communities through poetry, sound, film and collective storytelling.

In our first session, we will explore the theme of witness—how it resides at the intersection of the personal and the political, capturing both the unspoken and the unforgettable with a simple, generous act. We will challenge ourselves to ask: What do we overlook? How can we make more room to notice? How do we become aware of what we don’t yet see?

Together, we will discuss how we engage with living archives and how writing captures personal & collective experiences as they emerge in thought and take shape in poetic form. The poetry of witness is historically significant, complex, and multifaceted, yet fluid, nonlinear, and expansive. This session highlights the work of poets who write from specific historical contexts, using their lived experiences to shape expressions and sensibilities that embody their beliefs and truths, providing a lens to trace life’s imprints.
This session will be facilitated by Featured Poet Jedidiah Mugarura and Tender Possibilities’ founder, Farhia Tato.

Jedidiah Mugarura is a storyteller descended from the people of Nkore. Their storytelling seeks to find and reimagine the missing vowels to the songs we once sang before colonial violence, to project a future of agency and possibility for those still negotiating their bodies in empire.

title: Wounds with Jessica Kasiama
body: For the final session of Tender Possibilities at Allan Gardens, we will explore the theme of wounds through a collective and embodied approach. Together, we will read poems that invite us to uncover layers of meaning, vulnerability and resilience.

In this society, we have boundaries and rules for what counts as “real” pain. If the cause of your pain doesn’t fit within those boundaries, you have to graft on a new narrative based on the closest fit. Trauma is often depoliticized and hyper-individualized. Capitalist modernity itself is a wound—one that alters the very structure of perception and shifts how we relate to one another, to the land and to the systems that govern our lives.

By using poetry as a tool for inquiry, we will discuss how we might reframe our experiences, tending to the wounds we carry and imagining new possibilities for healing and collective care. This session will be facilitated by featured poet Jessica Kasiama and Tender Possibilities’ founder, Farhia Tato.

Jessica Kasiama is a writer, DJ, and bookseller. Building on Christina Sharpe’s framing of beauty as a practice, she seeks to preserve examples of this in Black music, movement, photography, and beyond. Through her written work, she aims to illuminate ways of being that promote care, safety, transformation, and belonging. Most urgently, she is a daughter and sister, shaped by stories and inquiries exchanged in these relationships.
Light refreshments will be provided by Krish (@cookeduntiltender)
RSVP here

title: Uncertainty (2024 Poet-in-Residence @ Gallery TPW)
body: For the final gathering as the 2024 Poet-In-Residence, we will explore the theme of uncertainty—the tension between the unknown and the potential it holds. Inspired by the exhibition Precarious Joys (featuring works by Manuel Mathieu, Abraham Oghobase, and Nicholas Galanin), we’ll read poems that engage with interruption, incoherence, and surprise—examining these forces both as sources of fear and instability, and as fertile spaces for transformation and possibility.
Tender Possibilities will open with a meditative soundscape by Chuk Fent & Viktor Rei, offering a grounding moment for participants.

title: Gratitude with Subhanya Sivajothy
body: We’re excited to partner with Friends of Allan Gardens for this year’s fall programming!

Gratitude is the recognition of our vulnerability and dependence on others. It reminds us of the threads that connect us. When these threads—so often taken for granted—fray, gratitude becomes an attempt to symbolically repair them. However, as a public discourse, gratitude can easily slip into something more troubling: an acceptance of the systems that exploit us and perpetuate harm. Behind its warm edges lies the moralizing and silencing accusation of being ungrateful. What does it mean when gratitude is no longer a spontaneous emotional response, but something that is asked or expected of us?

In this session of Tender Possibilities, we will explore gratitude as solidarity, rather than as an acceptance of the world as it is. We will examine the risks we take and the care we give to each other in the fight for the world as it could be. In its purest form, gratitude is generative and transformative, possessing a spiritual quality that creates possibilities for growth and change. Like poetry, it can be expressed in many ways—through subtle gestures, quiet moments, or grand declarations. Through readings and discussions, we will reflect on how gratitude appears in our lives, how it can inspire and sustain us, and how it can be subversive—offering new ways to understand and appreciate the world around us.
This session will be facilitated by featured poet Subhanya Sivajothy and Tender Possibilities’ founder, Farhia Tato.

Subhanya Sivajothy is a poet and librarian living in Tkarón:to. She uses poetry to think about ecologies, archives, and resistance and is the author of the chapbook Singing Fish Notation. She completed her MFA at University of Guelph. She has been published in magazines such as Adi Magazine, The Ex-Puritan and Filling Station.
Light refreshments will be provided by Krish (@cookeduntiltender)
Flyer designed by @bae_aulenti
RSVP here

title: Dreams with Tina Zafreen Alam
body: We’re excited to partner with Friends of Allan Gardens for this year’s fall programming! In our first session, we’ll explore the radical potential of dreams and the power of collective dreaming as acts of care.

Dreams are powerful forces within us, serving as vital sources of hope, healing, and imagination. In this session, we’ll focus on dreams as a third space—a liminal realm where we can process unresolved thoughts, connect with ancestors, and engage in meaningful dialogue with our inner selves.

Through curated poems, we’ll navigate dreamscapes, opening pathways for personal and shared understanding. This gathering will also honor the importance of slowing down and reconnecting with ourselves, emphasizing the significance of quiet moments—like daydreaming and silence—as essential acts of restoration and renewal.
This session will be facilitated by featured poet Tina Zafreen Alam and Tender Possibilities’ founder, Farhia Tato.

Tina Zafreen Alam is a diasporic Bangladeshi poet who does not believe in space, time, or borders. You can find her poems in FreezeRay Poetry, Voicemail Poems, Seventh Wave Magazine, Apogee Journal and The American Poetry Review. She is calling on you to commit your heart, body, and soul to fighting for the liberation of Palestine and of all oppressed people around the globe. We owe it to ourselves, and to one another. Revolution until complete liberation for all of us, all together.
Special thanks to Design Justice Network (DJN) for funding this session and for their continued support. We’re honoured to be part of DJN’s “Care May Be” Hybrid Gathering (Oct 21 - 27) ✨
Light refreshments will be provided by @cookeduntiltender
RSVP here

title: Defiance (2024 Poet-in-Residence @ Gallery TPW)
body:
For the spring session of the residency, we will explore the theme of defiance.

Inspired by Jane Jin Kaisen’s exhibition Burial of This Order, the curated selection of poems highlight collective empowerment, illustrating how individual and community rituals ignite processes of transformation.

Tender Possibilities will commence with a live meditative soundscape by Chuk Fent, inviting participants into a space of contemplation and introspection. Together, we'll reflect on how poetry can challenge traditional norms and unveil alternative narratives, echoing the exhibition's exploration of dismantling oppressive systems.

Capacity is limited. RSVP here.

title: COOPER COLE
body:
We are excited to host a session of Tender Possibilities at COOPER COLE, as part of the gallery's public programming for Hangama Amiri’s exhibition ‘Circle of Friends.’

We will be reading poems about collective memory. How our lived experiences disrupt colonial histories and confront oppression with its silences and exclusions. How memory can confront the linear ordering or geographies of containment that capital ascribes. As your facilitator, I will offer historical contexts but will mostly hold space for your personal reflections. Together, we will consider what can happen when we move deeply into and out from the language of a poem.
RSVP

title: Inheritance (2024 Poet-in-Residence @ Gallery TPW)
body: For the first session of the residency, we present 'inheritance' as our central theme. Through a curated selection of poems, we will delve into questions of personal agency, inherited trauma, and intergenerational transmission. Inspired by Meera Margaret Singh’s exhibition, What We Hold, the poems will serve as conduits of remembrance, bridging the gap between the past and present, and delving into generational trauma, familial histories, inherited memory and intergenerational connections.

title: Last Outdoor Session of 2023!
body: Please join us for our last session of the year! We will be reading about the poetics of refusal. The current political moment demands it. As we find our bearings in the present, it is clear that social and political terrains have shifted for many around the world. If refusal is continually appearing in the present moment as creative and potent, then our job is to consider how and why. Refusal is a practice.
If you sent your email last week, you’re already confirmed—anyone else who’d like to attend please e-mail info@tenderpossibilities.ca

title: Fire Pit Sessions Begin!
body: We are in a new location for our Fall outdoor sessions. Join us at Dufferin Grove Park (South Fire Pit), we will be reading poems about ghosts.
To register please e-mail info@tenderpossibilities.ca

title: Good Mourning Festival
body: Our belief is that grief is a profound expression of love that acknowledges the transformative impact of loss. Join us as we explore the healing potential of poetry within the realms of mourning.
